INTRODUCTION
The topic of this dissertation came about when I observed an interesting,
and apparently contradictory, phenomenon among many of my Hong Kong
Chinese friends in London. In a culture where social gatherings take place over
food rather that drink, I had noticed that having Chinese food was the first choice
of cuisine both for eating out and at home. This was completely opposite to
habits of friends that I had observed in Hong Kong, where young people eating
out would very rarely choose Cantonese food, opting instead for an array of
mostly Asian but also Western cuisines which in the city are familiar, accessible
and affordable.
For example dim sum in Hong Kong is a popular Sunday afternoon meal
for the entire family, these restaurants are also a favourite of retirees as it allows
them to sit and read the paper in the mornings. However a group of young
people in Hong Kong would almost never go out to for dim sum together; but in
London it is quite a popular activity.
This apparently paradoxical behavior piqued my interest in the role of
food not only in a person’s day-to-day habits, but also in the identity and situated
lifestyle they create for themselves. I decided to focus my research on young
Hong Kong Chinese living in London, to be able to contextualize my topic
amongst literature on modern migration. Through observing the consumption,
sharing and making Chinese food by Hong Kong migrants living in London, I will
consider how a cosmopolitan identity is enacted in a foreign place and all its
complexities, as well as the home that is created as a result of embodied
practices.

I hope that in a broader sociological context, this dissertation’s study of
the food habits of young Hong Kong Chinese migrants may contribute a small
part to the body of sociological literature on migration in the UK and London.
While there has been a lot written and published on the black community, the
South Asian
1
community, and other European migrant groups, East and
Southeast Asian
2
groups have been considerably less scrutinized.
I would speculate that this is not only because of the relatively small
number of East Asian migrants in the UK, especially compared to North America.
It is also because East Asians are generally seen as non-threatening by host
populations; mainly physically, due to smaller physical statures and a culture of
being non-confrontational; aside from any kung-fu references made jokingly.
East Asians generally speaking do not have strong religious or political beliefs,
which also makes them non-threatening culturally. Economically speaking, East
Asians due to relatively small numbers do not seem to be perceived as a threat;
younger migrants also tend to assimilate well into the Western professional
work force. However, with China’s recent economic boom and the increased
mobility of large numbers of Mainland Chinese, both as tourists or migrants, and
a generally higher profile of China and Asia in the media, this may not be true for
much longer.
I will now briefly consider the existing literature on different migrant and
ethnic groups living in the UK. Li Wei (1994) in Three Generations, two languages,
one family: language choice and language shift in a Chinese community in Britain
says that it is well-known, ‘almost a cliché’, that Chinese are among the least

economic impact may also account for less academic attention paid to Chinese

Regarding existing literature dealing with Chinese migrants:
‘Transnational Chinese: Fujianese Migrants in Europe’ (Pieke, 2004) is an
ethnographic study of Chinese migrants in Europe, focusing particularly on
Britain, Italy and Hungary as migration destinations, as well as in Fujian in China.
Focusing on Fujianese migrants and communities, the book looks at the meaning
of Chinese globalization as a global flow and ongoing process and predicts that
these flows are becoming more significant in the global landscape.
From a broader historical perspective, ‘Chinese Transnationalism in
Britain: A Longer History’ (Benton, 2003) takes a transnational studies approach
to early history of the British Chinese community, questioning the assumption
that most migrant economic ties are bottom-up and newly forged, by looking at
the role of transnational ties and political elites, which actually played a
significant role in the early migrant economy.
The simply titled ‘The Chinese in Britain’ (Chan and Chan, 1997) is a brief
history of Hong Kong migration to the UK, covering the opium war, the
oppression and violence following the June Fouth Incident and the pre-handover
migration rush in the 1990’s when many Hong Kong residents looked overseas
to protect their own interests.
There are some more up-to-date studies that look at young migrants and
technological permutations of culture, such as: ‘Ethnicity, Social Capital and the
Internet: British Chinese websites’ (Parker and Song, 2013), which researches
the social capital of second-generation Chinese migrants through websites
developed to express their interests and experiences. ‘Satellite TV and Chinese
5
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
Migrants in Britain (Lee, 2014) is an ethnographic study of the process and
politics of satellite television engenders identity formation amongst Hong Kong
Chinese migrants in the UK, and the differences in this process across
generations.
Women-focused studies provide some interesting insights into the
nuances of migrant lives, such as ‘Chinese migrant women and families in Britain’
(Lee et al, 2002), which looks at the contemporary life stories of women
migrants of varying economic and cultural backgrounds. ‘Husband’s career first:
renegotiating career and family commitment among migrant Chinese academic
couples in Britain’ (Cooke, 2007) is very niche study of trailing spouses; it also
points out the limited available literature on Chinese migrant employment in
Britain, particularly of female professionals.
‘Global and local articulations of Asian identity’ (Song, 2005) focuses on
East Asians in America, and the scope of the study highlights the lack of a
comparable one on the UK. Song says that the complexity of migration histories
means that migrant identity requires a decoupled understanding of a cultural
and national or ethnic identity. She then goes on to illustrate this with examples
of migrants that are unable to find common ground with people from their places
of origin; multi-generational migrants that look down on those that are ‘fresh off
the boat’; and issues facing returning migrants after many years abroad.
Overall, existing literature mostly seems to focus on the history of Chinese
migration to the UK, and there are only sporadic studies that deal with key
aspects of life and challenges faced by the contemporary Chinese migrant
population.

0.1 Methods
For this dissertation, my primary method of collecting data is through
conducting interviews and participant observation. The interviews were all
conducted over coffee or a meal and I did not have a set list of questions to go
through. I tried my best to keep the conversation as informal and free-flowing as
possible, using the immediate settings, conversational cues as well as
information and preferences gleaned from previous interviews as a guide; I
would also ask for stories to do with food and food habits. As all of my research
participants were already known to me as friends or acquaintances, arranging
interviews was simply a matter of getting in touch via telephone or the usual
channels of social media.
I also invited myself to dinner at two Hong Kong Chinese couples’ homes,
to observe their preparations and eating habits, as well as to conduct informal
interviews, or ‘steered conversations’ in a similar style to one-on-one interviews
described above during preparation and while sharing their meal. I would also
bring a Chinese dish I that I had made to reciprocate their hospitality.
Lastly I arranged a group pot-luck dinner which was attended by a mix of
participants that had taken part in earlier interviews and dinners and new
participants. I cooked a few dishes for my guests and also asked them to prepare
or bring a Chinese dish of their own; they also used my kitchen to prepare or
reheat their own dishes. During the dinner, I asked participants to introduce
their own dishes and talk about its preparation and why they chose it. I found
through my fieldwork, that the processes of making food and eating together was
often as, if not more informative than just talking about food.
7
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
(photo of dinner table at potluck, 29/6/2014)
In ‘A Sense of Place, A Sense of Time’, the authors (Vannini et al, 2012, p.
109) consider how food and eating, through our senses, shapes our engagement
with the self, others and the world. Sensing food, whether it is through sight,
smell, touch or taste, is a method of gathering information about the space and
culture of the society it is in. The authors criticize food scholars for making their
study of food a purely intellectual activity, rarely preparing or eating the food
they write about. They say ‘since eating is necessary for thinking, a more
appetizing sociological treatment of food should blend analysis with sensory
attention to – among other topics—its ingredients, the work involved in
8
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
producing it, the complex social practices surrounding its consumption, and, of
course, its taste’.
Throughout interviews and fieldwork, I found Les Back’s (2007)
introductory chapter in The Art of Listening to be very helpful. In particular, he
writes about listening as not a specific action, but being open to voices, and also
background and half muted noises. Back also says that while sociology is often
drawn to the most spectacular issues of the most acute social concerns, the
loudness or sensationalism of issues are relative, and therefore quieter issues are
also worthy of attention. In researching everyday habits surrounding food, I did
indeed discover that even mundane details could be quite illuminating.
Coming from an anthropological background, Back (ibid., p. 9) urges
researchers to pay attention not only to what is said, but also to the ‘hidden life
of objects and places’. He emphasizes a ‘commitment to engagement’, which
allows for a researcher to engage with participants in such a way that uncertain
or transient spaces of dialogue are opened up, most likely in their ordinary
places of life. I feel that the more congenial atmosphere during ‘research dinners’,
which requires more time and involvement on the part of the researcher, reflects
this theory. This also resonates with a point he makes later in the chapter (ibid., p.
17) that a common mistake students make while writing about their research is
to only quote the words of their subjects but not give context, which is equally
important, by describing the people or situation. I will aim to describe and
interpret as well as quote to present as full a picture as possible of what I have
observed.
As a researcher of the same ethnicity and background as my target
research group, it is important to note the possible advantages and
9
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
disadvantages. In ‘Ambivalent affect/ emotion’ (Saha and Watson, 2014), which
explores the ambivalences second-generation South Asian migrants feel towards
their own community, having two researchers of different ethnicities showed the
impact this can have in the field. The authors reflected that Saha, being of South
Asian decent himself, was able to share his own experiences of tensions within
his own community and therefore draw out those of his research subjects;
whereas for Watson, it was quite uncomfortable to speak of another community
in a way which would be perceived as negative (ibid., 101).
Since my research topic is perceived to be less sensitive socially and
politically, it may be that the outcomes of research conducted by a ‘native’
compared to ‘non-native’ researcher would not be a case of getting completely
contrasting data. However, I can still envisage quite a different outcome if a
researcher of another ethnicity or background were to conduct the same
research. Some obvious examples would be time spent explaining the various
foods and ingredients to a ‘foreigner’, or dinner table conversations held in
English rather than Cantonese. I do not want to say that it is a definite advantage
being of the same background and ethnicity, as what one gains in insider
knowledge and an immediate sense of belonging and acceptance equates
perhaps to loss of perspectives obtained from personal distance.
0.2 Target research group
Young Hong Kong Chinese migrants are a good example of a reasonably-
large, and generally well-educated and well-adapted migrant population in
London, in which such observed food preferences are a matter of choice rather
than necessity. I chose to comment specifically on education, as it means that
10
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
these individuals would be relatively well off, speak good English, and mostly
work in mainstream professions; and these are generally prerequisites for
smooth assimilation into a first-world, Western host population. It would also
imply that individuals have the tools as well as the curiosity to learn about
Western habits and lifestyles. I also use the term well-adapted because generally
speaking, Hong Kong migrants find it not too difficult to adapt to living abroad.
Amongst my research participants, a number have studied from a young age in
the UK, while others only migrated in adulthood. My participants are all white-
collar workers or professionals, and therefore by income and work nature would
identify as middle class. One could also speculate that Hong Kong having been a
British colony, there are certain social and cultural similarities; also Hong Kong
people themselves are not conservative in their own habits and lifestyle.
Indeed migration nowadays is not as permanent an undertaking for many
individuals as it once was; some reasons for this would include the ease and
lower cost of international travel, availability of information especially via the
Internet, and increasingly convenient banking and other personal administration
systems. Bauman (1997) in ‘Tourists and Vagabonds: the Heroes and Victims of
Postmodernity’ describes the two types of people that are globally mobile:
tourists who voluntarily adopt a lifestyle of travel and choose to make only
transient connections; and vagabonds that get swept along on the currents of
global movements and whose suffering allows the uncertainty in tourists’ lives to
seem bearable in comparison. The tourist and the vagabond are clearly
metaphoric and extreme examples. The type of migrant in my research would
definitely be more of a tourist than a vagabond.
11
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
It is quite clearly the case then that for young Hong Kong Chinese living in
London, they are quite capable socially, culturally and economically, of living a
Western lifestyle; and therefore it is their choice to seek out and consume
Chinese food on a regular basis while living abroad. It thus becomes an issue of
sociological taste that these migrants have chosen to express agency in the
matter of food.
Performances of taste, and considerations of cosmopolitanism and
authenticity of cuisines, as I will go on to discuss in the next section, are all
generally considered to be the concerns and characteristics of the middle class.
But because Hong Kong Chinese migrants in London cannot be considered fully
part of the British ‘class system’, the characteristics and implications of being
middle class are somewhat different. I have referred to ‘The Middle Class and
Xiao Kang Society’ (Lu, 2010), which discusses the characteristics of China’s
middle class, many of which are similar in the case of Hong Kong Chinese. In
China, people become middle class by means of occupation and economic status,
and unlike in the West, there is less social and cultural meaning associated with
the term (ibid., p. 107); the chapter also says that the relatively lower level of
class consciousness means that more individualistic factions of society, for
example entrepreneurs, have yet to develop a collective social identity (ibid., p.
121). As Hong Kong Chinese living abroad similarly form a small and new social
category, there is arguably space to create a new collective identity within the
middle class of the UK, Hong Kong, China or even globally.
0.3 Literature review
12
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
Existing literature tends to focus on the food practices of new migrants,
however they do not account for the lasting attachment to home foods even in
well-integrated second and third generation migrants, or those who came to the
UK as students at a formative age. However, traditional approaches such as
fuctionalism, structuralism and developmentalism, which I have first outlined
below, focus too much on finding rules and patterns that govern people’s food
choices and habits; whereas I believe while migrants may seem to display similar
food preferences, the reasons behind this can vary greatly for each individual,
and less prescriptive methods are called for in this case.
The first chapter of The Sociology of Food (Mennell et al, 1992) introduces
the traditional theories that explore the importance of food in society. The
approach of fuctionalism says that humans eat to survive and proposes a direct
link between food preferences and nutritional value. However, this has been
proven to be untrue in many cases, and for this research project irrelevant
because food choices are in fact overly abundant in a city like London. The
complex Chinese doctrines of 食療 (sik liu/ dietary medcine) also make this
theory inapplicable. Levi-Strauss and Douglas take a structuralist approach to
food: seeing meals as a fixed pattern that symbolize certain things to a certain
culture. Barthes similarly imposes the rules of grammar onto the meaning of
food choices. However, the structuralist approach is too prescriptive for
exploring the complex reasons behind food choices in migrant and multicultural
groups. Bourdieu looks for codes in food cultures that act as indicators of class
and sub-classes; however, this approach, like structuralism is quite prescriptive
and specific to western society. Theorists that are opposed to structuralism
moved onto developmentalism, such as Mennell who attempts to understand
13
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
how social, political and economic changes influence lifestyle and emotion, in
which food preferences and cuisines are an important part (ibid., p. 17).
However, the above theories do not sufficiently account for the many
variables and subtleties of modern day mobility, migration and movement;
where food can be the site of active growth and creations of migrants’ identities
and characteristics, not merely reproductions from their places of origin.
Therefore I will be focusing more on theories that relate to migrants’ sense of
home and identity, and extending current discussions to food and cuisine
popular amongst migrant Hong Kong Chinese in London.
Chapter 10 of ‘The Impact on Food of Colonization and Migration’ (ibid.,
pp. 75-78) gives a brief history of how foodstuffs and cuisines travelled with
migrants and became embedded in different localities. Communities of migrants
would try to maintain many of their original habits especially food; and in some
cases such as with Indian, Chinese and Italian cuisines, these dishes became
popular and accepted within the host population. Research into specific
immigrant groups’ food choices and habits that has been conducted would agree
that ethnicity, especially with first generation migrants, plays a large part in their
habits and choices. Food also is also used as a way to maintain ethnic and
cultural identity.
With young Hong Kong migrants in London today, they are often familiar
and comfortable with the language, lifestyle and food cultures of the West,
therefore the choice of ‘native’ cuisine is motivated more from preference than
necessity or even habit. In a more recent history of London’s Chinatown, young
Chinese seeking authentic tastes of home have become the main customer group
rather than Westerners wanting sweet and sour pork (Ming-Ai Institute, 2011).
14
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
David Sutton (2001) in Remembrances of Repasts does an ethnographic
study of how food plays a role in culture and memory on the Greek island of
Kalymnos. Food is central to the changing of the seasons, social events,
hospitality and even a touchstone to remembering details of days and
occurrences. Food evokes home for young migrants from Kalymnos, and the
rituals for preparation and equally as important; they are also a construction and
affirmation of cultural identity. Sutton also mentions concept of ‘synthesia’
relating to smell as a sense that is able to evoke rich memories and experiences. I
would add that taste, being closely related to smell, also has similar powers.
Sutton says there is ‘cultural variability in attitudes toward the relevance of the
“mundane” when it comes to food’ (ibid., p. 114). It is evident that the
Kalymnians place quite and high importance on food, and so, I would say, do the
Chinese.
The role that food and other sensory experiences play in memory and
preservation of culture is also the central theme of Nadia Seremetakis’ (1994)
The Senses Still. However, I also wish to look at the food preferences and
practices of young migrants as not only backward looking: as in evoking memory
and tradition, but also a practice that is active and current in formulating their
everyday identities and lifestyles.
In Chapter 4 of Everyday Multiculturalism (Khoo, 2009), the spaces of
Chinese-run coffee shops known as Kopitiam in Malaysia are explored as ‘third
spaces’ that form an important part of Malaysian Chinese’s social life and as
accessible gathering places for Malaysians of different cultural and religious
backgrounds. Yet food and alcohol restrictions are making these places off-limits
to many Muslim Malaysians nowadays, when the political climate has made the
15
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
ethnic and racial divide more strongly felt. What I found most pertinent in this
essay is the definition of a vernacular and international cosmopolitanism, as
evidenced by a Kopitiam in contrast to a Starbucks for example.
Applying the concept of cosmopolitanism to young Hong Kong Chinese in
London reveals an interesting dichotomy: when in Hong Kong, preferences are
for international, if still mostly Asian, cuisine; however when in London, good
and sometimes very traditional or even old-fashioned Cantonese food becomes
most sought-after. A more local sense of cosmopolitanism is evident in the more
generous definitions of Chinese food that will be discussed later in this
dissertation.
Khoo (ibid.) also points out that food places and the spaces in which
people choose to be are performances of identity. Chinatown restaurants are
almost kitsch representation of Chinese-ness and its food (Williams, 2014).
However the clientele is mainly Chinese, so perhaps they poke fun at these
overwhelming expressions of identity, but at the same time enjoy the familiarity
and shared understanding of the food and the familiar (lack of) atmosphere.
The ‘opposite’ phenomenon of Western food in Asia is explored in The
Golden Arches East (Watson, 1997) which delves into the many manifestations of
McDonald’s in East Asia; how the restaurant built its success on assimilating to
local cultures, and how local cultures adopted McDonald’s and enjoy it as
something quite different from what it was originally intended to be. In studying
the Chinese’s approach to a McDonald’s meal, the author received a lot of
feedback that a burger and fries did not make them feel full （吃不飽/ chi bu
16
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
bao
4
）, because buns are traditionally seen as snack food. In contrast a
Westerner would see a burger as predominately meat. It is an excellent example
of how cultural conceptions of food can yield completely different experiences of
it. The book concludes that food habits are deeply historical and social; so much
so that McDonalds, originally an American fast food restaurant, has become a
place for young people to leisurely hang out in Hong Kong, and a classy option
for dating and treating others to dinner in Beijing.
Similarly in this dissertation, I will ask how it is not only the perception of
Chinese food that is changed for inhabitants of a different city, but how the role
of the cuisine and the acts of preparing and eating that food becomes altered in
individuals’ everyday practices, enactments of identity, and in forming and
maintaining social relationships.
Consuming Geographies: We are Where We Eat (Bell and Valentine, 1997)
draws the link between food and locations, beginning from the body as the most
immediate location, and then home and moving outwards in ever-broader circles
to the community, city, to regional and national level and finally to global scale.
The book covers broad trends and attitudes regarding food, such as its
relationship to issues of class, ethnicity and cosmopolitanism. While it does not
go in depth into the many topics, which might well be impossible given the
broadness of the area that it covers, it does try to destabilize the often simplistic
assumptions and linkages made about food and for example nationality in
particular. In the final chapter, the authors propose thinking about food in terms
of ‘displacement’ or perpetual movement, where the food, its locality and socio-

cultural origins are all fluid (ibid, p. 200). It is a useful point to keep in mind
when thinking of Chinese food in London, which over time has arguably taken on
a life and character of its own, and is no longer ‘from’ Hong Kong or Guangdong
or China.
‘Immigrant entrepreneurs in advanced economies: mixed embeddedness
further explored’ (Kloosterman and Rath, 2001) is also about the changing roles
and functions of food and related resources in different locations in practicing
immigrant entrepreneurship. The importance of the demand or market side of
the equation that allows entrepreneurial activity to flourish is emphasized in this
paper, and it is analyzed in three layers: country, regional/ urban and
neighborhood. It is the combination of the immigrant entrepreneur’s social
embeddedness in their own networks and the condition of the market that
determines the viability of entrepreneurial activity. If this model can be extended
to other aspects of a migrant’s life, their food choices must also be seen in the
light of what is readily available to them in combination with the preferences and
habits.
The concept of mixed embeddedness as applied to a consumption point of
view is what I wish to take away from this paper. Native practices and networks
when existing in a foreign place take on different meanings and face different
challenges; however they retain a certain degree of linkage and similar
characteristics to their original form at home. It is interesting to consider the
degree to which Hong Kong Chinese’s food practices are ‘embedded’, and to what
extent the food and the environment of London each had to be adapted to
encompass the ‘mix’
18
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
Finally, Lisa Law (2001) in ‘Home Cooking: Filipino Women and
Geographies of the Senses in Hong Kong’ takes food as the central element of her
exploration of Filipino migrant domestic workers’ recreation of home and native
lifestyles. She quotes Seremetakis (1994) saying ‘a politics of sensory creation
[is] a politics of everyday life’, in exploring the practices of Filipino workers
preparing, sharing and eating their own food on Sundays as an embodied
practice; and at the same time producing a completely different sensory
landscape from that of everyday Hong Kong. The act of preparation, Law says,
becomes an active creation; and the practice of eating, often with hands rather
than utensils, is both productive and self-conscious. She also puts forth that food
may be a pertinent example of an ‘entangled object’ in terms of material culture’s
importance to contemporary cosmopolitan experience (pp. 234-235).
I will apply Law’s approach of observing as well as participating in the
consumption of food in this study. She emphasizes the importance of senses
other than taste including touch, smell and sound in creating a 360-degree
sensory landscape. In the article, the acts of preparation, sharing and eating are
also of equal importance in what has become a ritual to Filipino domestic
workers in Hong Kong, and these practices will also be looked at individually in
this study.
0.4 Structure
I did not start this dissertation with a hypothesis to test. My approach is
empirically led, therefore the structure and content has emerged out of themes
and concepts from data collected during fieldwork. My research participants’
explanations and explorations of their food practices can be broadly grouped
19
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
under the headings of ‘identity’ and ‘home’. While it is important to acknowledge
that these two chapters are deeply intertwined, for structural purposes I will
discuss more inward looking issues in the first chapter, and issues that touch on
not only home in a domestic sense, but also regarding community in the latter
chapter.
There are also recurring themes arising from fieldwork that run through
the chapters, these are cosmopolitanism, authenticity and considerations of
economic cost. Here I will briefly introduce theory and context of each.
While nostalgia would seem to be an obvious theme for a study about
migrant food habits, however it was not mentioned by most of my research
subjects. This may be due to the fact that the most common understanding of
nostalgia is backward looking, and indeed its translation in Chinese is 懷舊 (waai
gau), meaning literally holding on to the old. However Grunenberg (2014) in
‘This bridge is just like the one in Visegrad!’ offers a more constructive
understanding of nostalgia when discussing the food practices of Bosnian
refugees in Denmark. She rejects the notion of nostalgia as sticking to the past
and native ‘Bosnian’ identity as too narrow and simplistic, calling for an
understanding instead that allows nostalgic cultural practices to be seen as
performing and constituting identity and new ways of belonging and moving
forwards. She uses the example of pita making, which young women learn from
their mothers, to show that rituals or traditions change subtly with each
transmission, case in point that nostalgic practices are not stagnant. I will use
this understanding of nostalgia as a stabilising force for new ventures in this
dissertation.
20
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
0.4.1 Cosmopolitanism
‘Familiar and at ease in many different countries and cultures’
– the Oxford Online Dictionary
Etymologically it means ‘citizen of the world’. In the chapter 5, ‘City’, of
Consuming Geographies, Bell and Valentine (2001, p. 135) refer to Ulf Hannerz’s
description of the cosmopolitan as one who both masters, and to some extent
surrenders to an alien culture. He illustrates this with the example of people
eating cockroaches to immerse themselves in an exotic culture; and says that
such experiences as well as knowledge of ‘other’ cuisines will constitute a
‘globalised cultural capital’ (p. 135-136). This would seem to be the conventional
definition of cosmopolitanism, however it seems to be quite shallow, and also
euro-centric since it is not clear how it would apply to the people who’s own
cultures are perceived as exotic.
In the opening chapter of Stories of Cosmopolitan Belonging: Emotion and
location, ‘Moving and being moved’ (Jones et al, 2014), the authors look at the
definition of cosmopolitanism both in its application to the people they
researched and the overall approach of their study. They concluded in favour of
21
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
an open and fluid definition of cosmopolitanism, which has characteristics of
‘openness rather than fixity, of becoming rather than being, of pragmatism and
eclecticism, of critical thinking as well as material and political engagement, of
seeing the connection with the global or distant in the local and specific’. The
understanding of cosmopolitanism comes from Bradotti’s theory of nomadism,
which conceives of the world not as ‘things’, but as ‘processes’. The authors find a
slight issue with the term nomadic as the book is about ‘home’, however, since
their concept of home is not fixed, but a place that people come to belong to, the
idea of a process is also fitting (ibid., p. 6).
In this dissertation, I am interested in the concept of cosmopolitanism as a
value of an enacted identity and how that concept changes as individuals move
from one place to another, and as their relationship with those places change. It
would seem that in the scenario I have observed that cosmopolitanism for Hong
Kong Chinese at home is of the generic type: being comfortable and frequently
enjoying different cuisines. However in London, it may be argued that
cosmopolitanism is already demonstrated by living and fitting in in a foreign city;
therefore with regards to food, the homelike and familiar is pursued. I am also
hoping that through the empirical data collected, the concept of cosmopolitanism
can be shown to be one that can constantly produce new meaning, rather than
one that is tied to an inflexible mainstream culture.
0.4.2 Authenticity
‘made or done in the traditional or original way, or in a way that faithfully
resembles the original’

– The Oxford Online Dictionary
However, as it can be seen illustrated in the conversation during the
potluck dinner quoted below, the origins of dishes and cuisines are unclear and
constantly evolving. Consider also the authenticity of prawn toast for example, it
is authentic London Chinese, however might not be recognized at all in Hong
Kong.
P: So po kok chicken (a popular Cantonese dish known as ‘Portuguese
chicken’) does not exist is po kok (Portugal)…
K: No, or quite rarely. They eat seafood mostly
S: Nando’s ! it was opened by Portuguese..
P: So the real po kok chicken is Nandos
KY: But Nando’s should be based on African chicken: the piri piri sauce
K: … South African I think…
P: So the po kok chicken travelled all the way via India, where it picked up
curry sauce... then in Macau it was all mixed up …
HH: It got curry sauce first... then got coconut milk from Indonesia…
KY: What about Portuguese tarts?
K: They are really from Portugal
S: What about egg tarts?
P: They are from custard tarts
LL: But using water instead..
P: Because custard (milk?) was expensive…
E: And they should not be made with puff pastry
KY: Egg tarts and mainly egg with water... and Portuguese tarts are mostly
double cream with egg.
P: But egg tarts’ base is like custard tarts
K: It is only when they were bastardised they had a puff pastry base
I have observed that while eating out or trying to recreate a Chinese dish,
a frequent comment will be whether the dish is like (those at home): ‘好似啊’
(hou ci aa) means ‘it is very similar’, while the subject is conveniently left out. It
would seem to be the case then that the authenticity of Chinese foods
encountered abroad are more heavily scrutinized for authenticity. Or even
23
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
assumed by many to be inauthentic, leading to an exclamation of pleasant
surprise when it actually resembles the ‘real thing’.
In Consuming Geographies (Bell and Valentine, 2001), the authors discuss
how people have to prove that they are adventurous and knowledgeable about
certain exotic cuisines to construct a cosmopolitan identity, as it is understood in
an everyday capacity. Knowing what is authentic is seen as a mark of superior
knowledge and experience. This more generic usage of cosmopolitanism here, as
well as authenticity, are fixed values to aspire to, and most likely Eurocentric and
can be applied to extreme version of the tourist (Bauman, 1997). However, I
would argue that authenticity, while it is an attribute that is much discussed, also
is not a fixed concept.
‘Going for an Indian’ (Buettner, 2008) traces the history of South Indian
restaurants in the UK from curry houses to up-market restaurants. In looking at
the history of how Indian food became widely popular in Britain, Chicken Tikka
Masala is the ultimate example of a widely accepted modified dish: the addition
of masala sauce was to satisfy British customers. Buettner briefly mentions
authenticity, quoting Spooner (ibid., p. 883) in saying ‘authenticity is never
simply an objective measurement but rather is determined by the choices and
desires of persons seeking to establish, or strengthen, an elevated social position’.
This definition would seem to apply to cases of judging food and practices
and displaying knowledge about cuisines other than one’s own, however, the
pursuit of authenticity of one’s own cuisine in a foreign place would seem to be
less of an attempt to elevate oneself, but more of a collaborative effort to
discover and create certain tastes that are associated with home.
24
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
In instances of home cooking, the relative cost and effort in procuring
authentic ingredients will mean that my participants routinely use substitute
ingredients easily found in mainstream supermarkets. And while ‘good’ or
‘authentic’ Chinese restaurants maybe recommended amongst Hong Kong
Chinese in London and become frequented favourites, there is a sense that
Chinese food in London will never entirely be authentic. However, I think that
authenticity cannot be taken too seriously, as this would mean one would be
forever criticizing. I will illustrate later in this dissertation how the concept of
authenticity in the hands of new migrants is pliable and changing.
0.4.3 Economic cost
During fieldwork, I noticed that the cost of food would be mentioned very
early on in the conversation whether it was regarding purchasing ingredients or
eating out, generally as a second or third comment. I would speculate that there
are two reasons for this: first is that London has a reputation for being very
expensive, and in contrast, Hong Kong and Asia in general is known for being
cheap to eat out in
5
. Therefore the cost of food is readily on one’s mind.
Amongst the Chinese there is the concept of value-for-money （底/ dai）,
which also incorporates an element of feeling that one has out-smarted others,
usually the seller, which would add enjoyment to a meal; in the case of living in a
foreign city, the feeling may also come from overcoming import costs and other
economic implications when a bargain is found. Some of my research
5
However, this may no longer be the case, as due to rapid inflation in recent years, a
low-cost meal in Hong Kong has gone from being roughly two to three pounds to more
than four pounds.
25
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
participants have also said that the concept of very expensive or gourmet meals
seems to be at odds with Chinese food, such as paying fifty pounds for a roast
duck at Hutong. I would say the concept even goes beyond financial cost and
becomes an intrinsic element of the food and consequently its enjoyment.
Bourdieu’s (1997) study in ‘Distinction: a social critique of the judgment
of taste’ shows a consistent correlation between levels of cultural and economic
capital and the types of food typically consumed as well as the amounts people
were willing to spend on food. In the case of the subjects I interviewed, there is a
sense of pride in being able to purchase ingredients at low prices, and when
eating out, doing so for a ‘good’ price. They are also more reluctant than Western
counterparts to spend extra on gourmet or specialist, for example organic,
ingredients. Cost and thrift are not treated with the same embarrassment
commonly seen among the British, and evidence of thrifty habits is strong in my
research although my participants are not under financial pressure and generally
would identify as middle class.
Economic cost is not a theme that will be discussed in depth in this
dissertation, however I felt it important to briefly explore it due to its central role
in many Hong Kong Chinese migrants’ thinking about food.
